claim: Drosophila melanogaster uses smooth optomotor head and body movements to stabilize gaze.
source: Drosophila melanogaster uses smooth optomotor head and body movements to stabilize gaze, and impulsive saccades to pursue elongated vertical bars.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing established behavior of Drosophila.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster uses impulsive saccades to pursue elongated vertical bars.
source: Drosophila melanogaster uses smooth optomotor head and body movements to stabilize gaze, and impulsive saccades to pursue elongated vertical bars.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing established behavior of Drosophila.

claim: Directionally selective motion detectors T4 and T5 cells provide inputs to large-field neurons in the lobula plate.
source: Directionally selective motion detectors T4 and T5 cells provide inputs to large-field neurons in the lobula plate, which control optomotor gaze stabilization behavior.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical and functional connectivity in the Drosophila visual system.

claim: Large-field neurons in the lobula plate control optomotor gaze stabilization behavior.
source: Directionally selective motion detectors T4 and T5 cells provide inputs to large-field neurons in the lobula plate, which control optomotor gaze stabilization behavior.
evidence: This is a statement of established functional role of lobula plate neurons.

claim: T3 cells provide inputs to the lobula.
source: Here, we hypothesized that an anatomically parallel pathway represented by T3 cells, which provide inputs to the lobula, drives bar tracking body saccades.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical connectivity that is part of the hypothesis being tested.

claim: T3 neurons respond omnidirectionally to the same visual stimuli that elicit bar tracking saccades.
source: We combined physiological and behavioral experiments to show that T3 neurons respond omnidirectionally to the same visual stimuli that elicit bar tracking saccades, silencing T3 reduced the frequency of tracking saccades, and optogenetic manipulation of T3 acted on the saccade rate in a push–pull manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing T3 reduced the frequency of tracking saccades.
source: We combined physiological and behavioral experiments to show that T3 neurons respond omnidirectionally to the same visual stimuli that elicit bar tracking saccades, silencing T3 reduced the frequency of tracking saccades, and optogenetic manipulation of T3 acted on the saccade rate in a push–pull manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic manipulation of T3 acted on the saccade rate in a push–pull manner.
source: We combined physiological and behavioral experiments to show that T3 neurons respond omnidirectionally to the same visual stimuli that elicit bar tracking saccades, silencing T3 reduced the frequency of tracking saccades, and optogenetic manipulation of T3 acted on the saccade rate in a push–pull manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Manipulating T3 did not affect smooth optomotor responses to large-field motion.
source: Manipulating T3 did not affect smooth optomotor responses to large-field motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Parallel neural pathways coordinate smooth gaze stabilization and saccadic bar tracking behavior during flight.
source: Our results show that parallel neural pathways coordinate smooth gaze stabilization and saccadic bar tracking behavior during flight.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: Flies have shown a stunning ability to actively orient toward and fixate foreground object stimuli, specifically long vertical bars.
source: Flies have shown a stunning ability to actively orient toward and fixate foreground object stimuli, specifically long vertical bars, using detection algorithms that rely on few parameters and are remarkably robust to perturbation (Egelhaaf, 1985; Reichardt et al., 1983; Theobald et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Flies use detection algorithms that rely on few parameters and are remarkably robust to perturbation for bar orientation behavior.
source: Flies have shown a stunning ability to actively orient toward and fixate foreground object stimuli, specifically long vertical bars, using detection algorithms that rely on few parameters and are remarkably robust to perturbation (Egelhaaf, 1985; Reichardt et al., 1983; Theobald et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bar orientation behavior becomes more challenging during locomotion when the visual scene moves across the retina generating complex patterns of optic flow.
source: Bar orientation behavior becomes more challenging during locomotion when the visual scene moves across the retina generating complex patterns of optic flow that can move with or opposite the direction of the pursued bar (Fox et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: T4 and T5 are parallel ON and OFF directional motion detectors.
source: Small-field sampling of the visual world culminates in parallel ON and OFF directional motion detectors T4 and T5, respectively (Joesch et al., 2010; Strother et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T4 and T5 columnar neuron classes each have four subtypes tuned to a singular cardinal direction.
source: These two columnar neuron classes each have four subtypes tuned to a singular cardinal direction, which innervate one of four direction-selective layers of the lobula plate, the third neuropil of the optic lobe (Fisher et al., 2015; Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T4 and T5 subtypes innervate one of four direction-selective layers of the lobula plate.
source: These two columnar neuron classes each have four subtypes tuned to a singular cardinal direction, which innervate one of four direction-selective layers of the lobula plate, the third neuropil of the optic lobe (Fisher et al., 2015; Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interneurons of the lobula plate pool inputs from T4/T5 cells to assemble complex spatial filters for patterns of optic flow.
source: Interneurons of the lobula plate pool inputs from T4/T5 cells to assemble complex spatial filters for patterns of optic flow and project their axons to pre-motor descending pathways that have been proposed to coordinate directional head and wing steering movements to stabilize gaze against perturbations during locomotion (Busch et al., 2018; Haikala et al., 2013; Heisenberg et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lobula plate interneurons project their axons to pre-motor descending pathways that have been proposed to coordinate directional head and wing steering movements to stabilize gaze against perturbations during locomotion.
source: Interneurons of the lobula plate pool inputs from T4/T5 cells to assemble complex spatial filters for patterns of optic flow and project their axons to pre-motor descending pathways that have been proposed to coordinate directional head and wing steering movements to stabilize gaze against perturbations during locomotion (Busch et al., 2018; Haikala et al., 2013; Heisenberg et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A motion opponency mechanism uses a group of lobula plate inhibitory interneurons to attenuate visual signals unrelated to self-motion.
source: A motion opponency mechanism uses a group of lobula plate inhibitory interneurons to attenuate visual signals unrelated to self-motion (Mauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The directional motion vision system is well suited to control optomotor gaze stabilization.
source: Hence, the directional motion vision system is well suited to control optomotor gaze stabilization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the preceding description of the directional motion vision system.

claim: The cellular mechanisms for coordinating bar tracking (i.e., exafferent motion) remain poorly understood.
source: Yet, the cellular mechanisms for coordinating bar tracking (i.e., exafferent motion) remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Identifying foreground objects from a cluttered background requires some visual computations that either are not supported by or do not require the directional motion vision system.
source: Identifying foreground objects from a cluttered background requires some visual computations that either are not supported by or do not require the directional motion vision system (Aptekar and Frye, 2013; Reichardt et al., 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several studies show that silencing directional motion detectors has little impact on object orientation behavior.
source: Several studies show that silencing directional motion detectors has little impact on object orientation behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of prior research findings.

claim: In tethered walking flies, synaptic suppression of T4/T5 cells dramatically reduces responses to bar motion but leaves orientation responses toward a stationary flickering bar largely unaffected.
source: For example, in tethered walking flies, synaptic suppression of T4/T5 cells dramatically reduces responses to bar motion but leaves orientation responses toward a stationary flickering bar largely unaffected (Bahl et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In tethered flying flies, revolving a textured vertical bar around a textured circular arena generates a distinct initial steering response oriented counter directional to the moving bar, followed by a secondary response in the same direction of bar motion.
source: In tethered flying flies, revolving a textured vertical bar around a textured circular arena generates a distinct initial steering response oriented counter directional to the moving bar, followed by a secondary response in the same direction of bar motion (Keleş et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Silencing T4/T5 under conditions of a revolving textured bar reduced the secondary syn-directional tracking response, but left the initial counter-directional orientation phase intact.
source: Silencing T4/T5 under these conditions reduced the secondary syn-directional tracking response, but left the initial counter-directional orientation phase intact (Keleş et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A separate direction-independent subsystem that detects spatial contrast properties rather than motion direction per se might play a role in object orientation.
source: These results would imply that a separate direction-independent subsystem that detects spatial contrast properties rather than motion direction per se might play a role in object orientation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of prior studies.

claim: Peripheral circuits have been shown to encode the requisite spatial contrast information.
source: Peripheral circuits have been shown to encode the requisite spatial contrast information (Bahl et al., 2015; Bahl et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Yaw-free flies execute rapid body saccades to track a revolving narrow vertical bar.
source: Under these conditions, yaw-free flies execute rapid body saccades to track a revolving narrow vertical bar.
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior in a specific experimental paradigm.

claim: Yaw-free flies execute smooth steering movements to stabilize a revolving large-field panorama.
source: By contrast, they execute smooth steering movements to stabilize a revolving large-field panorama; smooth optomotor movement is interspersed with occasional nystagmus saccades or syn-directional 'catch up' saccades (i.e., optomotor saccades).
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior in a specific experimental paradigm.

claim: The dynamics of bar tracking saccades are distinct from large-field optomotor saccades.
source: But the dynamics of bar tracking saccades are distinct from large-field optomotor saccades (Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Perturbation of the directional motion vision pathway attenuates smooth optomotor responses.
source: Perturbation of the directional motion vision pathway attenuates smooth optomotor responses, whereas perturbation of the spatial contrast pathway would be expected to compromise bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a statement of expected outcomes based on the functional roles of different pathways.

claim: Perturbation of the spatial contrast pathway would be expected to compromise bar tracking saccades.
source: Perturbation of the directional motion vision pathway attenuates smooth optomotor responses, whereas perturbation of the spatial contrast pathway would be expected to compromise bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a statement of expected outcomes based on the functional roles of different pathways.

claim: Elongated vertical bars resemble plant stalks on which flies land.
source: Here, we investigate a candidate pathway for object tracking by focusing on the response to elongated vertical bars that have been shown to provoke attractive orientation behavior in flying flies because they resemble plant stalks on which to land (Maimon et al., 2008; Mongeau et al., 2019; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Elongated vertical bars provoke attractive orientation behavior in flying flies.
source: Here, we investigate a candidate pathway for object tracking by focusing on the response to elongated vertical bars that have been shown to provoke attractive orientation behavior in flying flies because they resemble plant stalks on which to land (Maimon et al., 2008; Mongeau et al., 2019; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T4/T5 coordinate smooth large-field optomotor responses that stabilize visual gaze.
source: We confirm previous lines of evidence that T4/T5 coordinate smooth large-field optomotor responses that stabilize visual gaze and go substantially further to show that a parallel neural pathway, comprising T3 neurons, controls bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a confirmation of prior findings and a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: A parallel neural pathway, comprising T3 neurons, controls bar tracking saccades.
source: We confirm previous lines of evidence that T4/T5 coordinate smooth large-field optomotor responses that stabilize visual gaze and go substantially further to show that a parallel neural pathway, comprising T3 neurons, controls bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: T3 neurons arborize within single columns of the medulla and send axons into layers 2 and 3 of the lobula.
source: T3 neurons arborize within single columns of the medulla and send axons into layers 2 and 3 of the fourth neuropil of the fly optic lobe, the lobula (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T3 neurons have previously been shown to respond to either small square objects or long vertical bars.
source: These neurons have previously been shown to respond to either small square objects or long vertical bars (Keleş et al., 2020; Tanaka and Clark, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T3 neurons respond vigorously to the camouflaged motion-defined bars that robustly elicit tracking saccades.
source: Using calcium imaging, we demonstrate that T3 neurons respond vigorously to the camouflaged motion-defined bars that robustly elicit tracking saccades (Mongeau et al., 2019; Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In rigidly tethered flies, hyperpolarizing T3 by genetically expressing an inward rectifier potassium channel (Kir2.1) reduces the initial counter-directional orientation response typically deployed for tracking motion-defined bars.
source: In rigidly tethered flies, hyperpolarizing T3 by genetically expressing an inward rectifier potassium channel (Kir2.1) reduces the initial counter-directional orientation response typically deployed for tracking motion-defined bars.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In magnetically tethered flies, hyperpolarizing T3 neurons reduces the frequency of bar tracking saccades.
source: In magnetically tethered flies, hyperpolarizing T3 neurons reduces the frequency of bar tracking saccades, whereas ON-OFF optogenetic activation by CsChrimson modulates a push–pull mechanism on saccade frequency.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: ON-OFF optogenetic activation of T3 by CsChrimson modulates a push–pull mechanism on saccade frequency.
source: In magnetically tethered flies, hyperpolarizing T3 neurons reduces the frequency of bar tracking saccades, whereas ON-OFF optogenetic activation by CsChrimson modulates a push–pull mechanism on saccade frequency.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Ensemble T3 activity can trigger bar tracking saccades through a behaviorally relevant integrate-and-fire mechanism.
source: Finally, based on T3's physiological properties and the behavioral dynamics of bar tracking (Mongeau and Frye, 2017), we propose a model for how ensemble T3 activity can trigger bar tracking saccades through a behaviorally relevant integrate-and-fire mechanism (Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the physiological data and prior behavioral findings.

claim: T3 showed an increase in calcium activity within individual presynaptic terminals when presented with bars of varying directions and contrast polarities moving across the right visual field.
source: T3 showed an increase in calcium activity within individual presynaptic terminals, and the ensemble of T3 dendrites innervating layer 9 of the medulla exhibited a robust retinotopic wave of activation as the bar swept across the retina (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The ensemble of T3 dendrites innervating layer 9 of the medulla exhibited a robust retinotopic wave of activation as the bar swept across the retina.
source: T3 showed an increase in calcium activity within individual presynaptic terminals, and the ensemble of T3 dendrites innervating layer 9 of the medulla exhibited a robust retinotopic wave of activation as the bar swept across the retina (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3 neurons were strongly activated by front-to-back and back-to-front motion of either ON (brighter than background) or OFF (darker than background) bars, with a modest preference for OFF transitions.
source: Broadly consistent with prior results (Keleş et al., 2020), T3 neurons were strongly activated by front-to-back and back-to-front motion of either ON (brighter than background) or OFF (darker than background) bars, with a modest preference for OFF transitions (Figure 1D and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Average T3 RF size was mainly confined to the center 9° bin with almost no activity outside of it.
source: Average T3 RF size was mainly confined to the center 9° bin with almost no activity outside of it, which closely matched previous measurements (Tanaka and Clark, 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: T3 neurons were almost identically sensitive to leftward (back-to-front) and rightward (front-to-back) moving bars.
source: We found that T3 neurons were almost identically sensitive to leftward (back-to-front) and rightward (front-to-back) moving bars, as well as to upward and downward movements through the center of the RF, although with a higher variability to the latter (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3 neurons were sensitive to upward and downward movements through the center of the RF, although with a higher variability to the latter.
source: We found that T3 neurons were almost identically sensitive to leftward (back-to-front) and rightward (front-to-back) moving bars, as well as to upward and downward movements through the center of the RF, although with a higher variability to the latter (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5 respond more strongly to a solid luminance-defined bar by comparison to a motion-defined bar.
source: Note that T4/T5 respond more strongly to a solid luminance-defined bar by comparison to a motion-defined bar (Keleş et al., 2018) due to sensitivity for longer spatial wavelength stimuli (Agrochao et al., 2020; Groschner et al., 2022; Gruntman et al., 2019; Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T3 show rapid full-wave rectified response kinetics to flicker.
source: T3 show rapid full-wave rectified response kinetics to flicker (Keleş et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: T3 neurons responded strongly to motion-defined bars by comparison to solid ON and OFF bars.
source: As expected, T3 neurons responded strongly to these stimuli by comparison to solid ON and OFF bars (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: As bar speed increased, the T3 responses decreased both for motion-defined and solid OFF and ON bars.
source: As bar speed increased, the responses decreased both for motion-defined (Figure 1I) and solid OFF and ON bars (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T2a has a small RF and omnidirectional sensitivity similar to T3.
source: Similar to T3, T2a has a small RF and omnidirectional sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T2a showed strong responses to luminance-defined bars (with a preference for ON transitions) moving at a low speed (18° s–1), but not at behaviorally relevant higher speeds.
source: T2a showed strong responses to luminance-defined bars (with a preference for ON transitions) moving at a low speed (18° s–1), but not at behaviorally relevant higher speeds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T2a showed weak-to-no responses to motion-defined bars.
source: Moreover, T2a showed weak-to-no responses to motion-defined bars (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G) and large-field gratings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T2a showed weak-to-no responses to large-field gratings.
source: Moreover, T2a showed weak-to-no responses to motion-defined bars (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G) and large-field gratings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3 responses to unilateral large-field gratings were nonselective for motion direction.
source: Responses to unilateral large-field gratings were nonselective for motion direction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Stimulating with a unilateral large-field grating suggests that T3 neurons are not strictly object selective, even though center-surround mechanisms shape T3 RF properties.
source: Stimulating with a unilateral large-field grating, by comparison to the bilateral gratings used in prior work, suggests that T3 neurons are not strictly object selective, even though center-surround mechanisms shape T3 RF properties (Keleş et al., 2020; Tanaka and Clark, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior work.

claim: T3 responses to an λ = 18° grating moving at 2 Hz (36° s–1) were similar to the responses to an λ = 36° grating moving at 1 Hz (36° s–1), suggesting that response amplitude was tuned to stimulus speed.
source: Responses to an λ = 18° grating moving at 2 Hz (36° s–1) were similar to the responses to an λ = 36° grating moving at 1 Hz (36° s–1), suggesting that response amplitude was tuned to stimulus speed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The two spatial patterns presented at 90° s–1 produced identical amplitude responses in T3.
source: Similarly, the two spatial patterns presented at 90° s–1 produced identical amplitude responses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5 neurons are tuned to the ratio of speed to spatial wavelength, temporal frequency (TF-tuned), rather than to the true stimulus speed (speed-tuned).
source: Unlike T3, which appear to be selective for pattern speed independently of spatial wavelength, T4/T5 neurons are tuned to the ratio of speed to spatial wavelength, temporal frequency (TF-tuned), rather than to the true stimulus speed (speed-tuned).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about T4/T5 neurons.

claim: T3 neurons show a selectivity for speeds between 100° s–1 and 200° s–1 regardless of spatial wavelengths.
source: T3 neurons show a selectivity for speeds between 100° s–1 and 200° s–1 regardless of spatial wavelengths, whereas the TFs are more spread out depending on the spatial wavelengths.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Rigidly tethered flies respond to a bar revolving around a cylindrical visual display with a compound steering response composed of a counter-directional orientation component while the bar is in the visual periphery and a syn-directional tracking component while the bar crosses the visual midline.
source: Rigidly tethered flies respond to a bar revolving around a cylindrical visual display (Figure 3A) with a compound steering response composed of a counter-directional orientation component while the bar is in the visual periphery and a syn-directional tracking component while the bar crosses the visual midline (Keleş et al., 2018; Reiser and Dickinson, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of observed behavior supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Flies expressing inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 in T4/T5 neurons showed weakened syn-directional tracking responses, but intact counter-directional orientation responses.
source: Flies expressing inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1 (Baines et al., 2001) in T4/T5 neurons showed weakened syn-directional tracking responses, but intact counter-directional orientation responses (Keleş et al., 2018; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures, and also cites prior work.

claim: Compared to the responses of empty split-Gal4 crossed with UAS-Kir2.1, the counter-directional orientation responses of T3 silenced flies were significantly reduced, whereas T4/T5 silenced flies were unaffected.
source: Compared to the responses of empty split-Gal4 crossed with UAS-Kir2.1, the counter-directional orientation responses of T3 silenced flies were significantly reduced, whereas T4/T5 silenced flies were unaffected (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Flies with hyperpolarized T3 neurons responded to the revolving bar by always steering (ΔWBA) in the direction of motion.
source: On average, flies with hyperpolarized T3 neurons responded to the revolving bar by always steering (ΔWBA) in the direction of motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: As the bar crossed visual midline, T3 silenced flies seemed to 'anticipate' the bar (ΔWBA > 0 when the bar was at visual midline).
source: Thus, as the bar crossed visual midline, these animals seemed to 'anticipate' the bar (ΔWBA > 0 when the bar was at visual midline).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Controls and T4/T5 silenced flies showed an initial counter-directional orientation response, followed by a weakened syn-directional response so that steering is balanced (ΔWBA = 0) as the bar crossed midline.
source: By contrast, controls and T4/T5 silenced flies showed an initial counter-directional orientation response, followed by a weakened syn-directional response so that steering is balanced (ΔWBA = 0) as the bar crossed midline (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The T3 split-Gal4 driver line showed no cellular labeling elsewhere in the brain or ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: This phenotype was not biased by off-target expression because our T3 split-Gal4 driver line showed no cellular labeling elsewhere in the brain or ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: For bar stimuli that evoke significantly stronger syn-directional steering effort, such as a 30° solid dark bar, silencing T3 had no effect, whereas blocking T4/T5 neurons did.
source: For bar stimuli that evoke significantly stronger syn-directional steering effort, such as a 30° solid dark bar, silencing T3 had no effect, whereas, as shown previously (Keleş et al., 2018), blocking T4/T5 neurons did (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures, and also cites prior work.

claim: The typical advanced response generated by winding up the optomotor system, which is dependent on T4/T5 neurons, was intact in T3 silenced flies.
source: Confirming the results of Figure 3, the typical advanced response generated by winding up the optomotor system, which is dependent on T4/T5 neurons, was intact in T3 silenced flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Synaptic silencing of T4/T5 reduced the turning toward small dark objects moving back-to-front.
source: Synaptic silencing of T4/T5 reduced the turning toward small dark objects moving back-to-front (Tanaka and Clark, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Virtual closed-loop bar fixation experiments have shown to depend on T4/T5 neurons.
source: Moreover, virtual closed-loop bar fixation experiments have shown to depend on T4/T5 neurons (Fenk et al., 2014), but silencing T3 had no effect on this behavior regardless of the type of bar (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and experimental data.

claim: Silencing T3 had no effect on virtual closed-loop bar fixation behavior regardless of the type of bar.
source: Moreover, virtual closed-loop bar fixation experiments have shown to depend on T4/T5 neurons (Fenk et al., 2014), but silencing T3 had no effect on this behavior regardless of the type of bar (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: For rigidly tethered flies, the syn-directional optomotor tracking response to a moving bar is dependent upon T4/T5 activity.
source: The parsimonious interpretation of these results is that, for rigidly tethered flies, the syn-directional optomotor tracking response to a moving bar is dependent upon T4/T5 activity, whereas the counter-directional orientational response is dependent upon T3 activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: For rigidly tethered flies, the counter-directional orientational response is dependent upon T3 activity.
source: The parsimonious interpretation of these results is that, for rigidly tethered flies, the syn-directional optomotor tracking response to a moving bar is dependent upon T4/T5 activity, whereas the counter-directional orientational response is dependent upon T3 activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Orientation responses by rigidly tethered flies and saccadic tracking responses by magnetically tethered flies are coordinated by non-directional (or omnidirectional) positional feature detectors with sensitivity to the high-frequency transients generated by motion-defined bars.
source: Behavioral results and theoretical models suggest that orientation responses by rigidly tethered flies and saccadic tracking responses by magnetically tethered flies are coordinated by non-directional (or omnidirectional) positional feature detectors with sensitivity to the high-frequency transients generated by motion-defined bars, naturalistic stimuli that might not strongly activate directional motion detectors (Keleş et al., 2018; Mongeau and Frye, 2017; Reichardt and Poggio, 1976).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: T3 cells show physiological properties consistent with non-directional positional feature detectors.
source: T3 cells indeed show these physiological properties (Figure 1 and 2) and are required for intact counter-directional orientation steering effort (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: T3 cells are required for intact counter-directional orientation steering effort.
source: T3 cells indeed show these physiological properties (Figure 1 and 2) and are required for intact counter-directional orientation steering effort (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: By visual inspection, controls dispersed within the first second, but T3 silenced flies remained concentrated at their initial heading, indicating that they were not tracking the motion-defined bar.
source: By visual inspection, controls dispersed within the first second, but T3 silenced flies remained concentrated at their initial heading, indicating that they were not tracking the motion-defined bar (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5 silenced flies dispersed similar to empty vector controls indicating that they were able to follow to some extent.
source: T4/T5 silenced flies dispersed similar to empty vector controls indicating that they were able to follow to some extent.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Both T3 and T4/T5 silenced flies showed a lower frequency of saccades than controls.
source: We next computed the frequency of body saccades during the trials, confirming the rate for our controls (~1 Hz) is in agreement with that of wild-type flies (Mongeau and Frye, 2017). Both T3 and T4/T5 silenced flies showed a lower frequency of saccades than controls, suggesting some role of both cell types (Figure 4C).

claim: T3 silenced flies showed a similar overall percentage of positive PI as controls, but the distribution of PI was very different for T3.

claim: T4/T5 showed more positive PI than controls.
source: Curiously, T4/T5 showed more positive PI than controls (Figure 4D, top), indicating that these flies were more inclined to steer syn-directionally with the bar.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Controls showed a negative correlation between initial bar position and resulting PI, meaning that when the bar starts from 180°, the flies tend to steer counter-directionally toward it (PI < 0).
source: Indeed, controls showed a negative correlation between initial bar position and resulting PI, meaning that when the bar starts from 180°, the flies tend to steer counter-directionally toward it (PI < 0), whereas, consistent with their small displacement response (Figure 4B), T3 silenced flies did not show any correlation between initial bar position and PI (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3 silenced flies did not show any correlation between initial bar position and PI.
source: Indeed, controls showed a negative correlation between initial bar position and resulting PI, meaning that when the bar starts from 180°, the flies tend to steer counter-directionally toward it (PI < 0), whereas, consistent with their small displacement response (Figure 4B), T3 silenced flies did not show any correlation between initial bar position and PI (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5 silenced flies showed a positive correlation between initial bar position and PI, meaning that they tended to steer in the direction of bar motion (PI > 0).

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Flies expressing Kir2.1 in T4/T5 showed average PI comparable to the controls.
source: Interestingly, flies expressing Kir2.1 in T4/T5 showed average PI comparable to the controls (Figure 4E), meaning that they were able to track the bar without performing as many saccades (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Silencing T4/T5 produced an overall increase of angular velocity by comparison with controls, especially when the bar was near the visual midline.
source: To delve further into this phenomenon, we measured the average angular velocity as a function of the bar position. Silencing T4/T5 produced an overall increase of angular velocity by comparison with controls, especially when the bar was near the visual midline (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The percentage of trials without any bar tracking bouts was higher in T3 hyperpolarized flies but equal between control and T4/T5 hyperpolarized flies.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: When bouts did occur, the average duration did not differ among genotypes, but their number of tracking bouts per trial was higher in T4/T5 silenced flies than controls.
source: When bouts did occur, the average duration did not differ among genotypes, but their number of tracking bouts per trial was higher in T4/T5 silenced flies than controls (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The silencing of T4/T5 led tendentially to higher inter-saccade tracking gain than controls and T3 silenced flies.
source: Finally, we analyzed the inter-saccadic gain (ratio of body rotation to stimulus rotation between saccades) during bar tracking bouts. The silencing of T4/T5 led tendentially to higher inter-saccade tracking gain than controls and T3 silenced flies (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Flies with silenced T4/T5 were 'pushed around' by the moving bar.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that flies with silenced T4/T5 were 'pushed around' by the moving bar.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Smooth bar tracking behavior is a result of the inability to properly stabilize the visual panorama in T4/T5 silenced flies.
source: This may seem counterintuitive since T4/T5 provide the directional motion signals for optomotor steering, so their blockade should be expected to attenuate smooth bar responses. Consider, however, that smooth bar tracking behavior is a result of the inability to properly stabilize the visual panorama in T4/T5 silenced flies.

claim: Following the bar resulted in extended pre-saccadic error angles for T4/T5 silenced flies.
source: Following the bar resulted in extended pre-saccadic error angles for T4/T5 silenced flies (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

source: The corollary is that integrating the bar error to trigger a saccade (Mongeau and Frye, 2017) requires stable visual gaze.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and prior work.

claim: Saccade amplitude was slightly reduced in both T3 and T4/T5 blocked flies.
source: However, saccade amplitude was slightly reduced in both T3 and T4/T5 blocked flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5 silenced flies showed higher percentage of trials with PI equal or less than zero (i.e., no stabilization), reduced positive PI value, and reduced smooth inter-saccadic gain in response to rotation of a full large-field panorama.
source: Silencing T4/T5 would be expected to compromise large-field optomotor gaze stabilization. We compared the silencing effects in response to rotation of a full large-field panorama, T4/T5 silenced flies showed higher percentage of trials with PI equal or less than zero (i.e., no stabilization), reduced positive PI value, and reduced smooth inter-saccadic gain (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).

claim: These effects are in agreement with a compromised directional optomotor system.
source: These effects are in agreement with a compromised directional optomotor system (Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by a citation.

source: It is noteworthy that hyperpolarization of T3 neurons did not affect large-field elicited gaze stabilization in any measurable way (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

source: Population depolarization of T4/T5 seemed not to change saccadic tracking in any obvious way (Figure 5B, bottom green, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The percentage of trials with PI > 0 (active bar tracking) was high in T3>CsChrimson flies when the light was OFF.
source: The percentage of trials with PI > 0 (active bar tracking) was high in T3>CsChrimson flies when the light was OFF (Figure 5C), whereas the same flies shifted to zero PI (no bar tracking) when the light was ON (Figure 5C), recapitulating the effect of the silencing manipulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3>CsChrimson flies shifted to zero PI (no bar tracking) when the light was ON.
source: The percentage of trials with PI > 0 (active bar tracking) was high in T3>CsChrimson flies when the light was OFF (Figure 5C), whereas the same flies shifted to zero PI (no bar tracking) when the light was ON (Figure 5C), recapitulating the effect of the silencing manipulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: CsChrimson activation had no obvious influence over the distribution of PI for T4/T5.
source: CsChrimson activation had no obvious influence over the distribution of PI for T4/T5.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Light-gated depolarization of T3 neurons caused cessation of bar responses before the first 360° revolution around the circular arena, whereas controls and T4/T5>CsChrimson flies, on average, continued to steer throughout the trial.
source: However, light-gated depolarization of T3 neurons caused cessation of bar responses before the first 360° revolution around the circular arena, whereas controls and T4/T5>CsChrimson flies, on average, continued to steer throughout the trial (Figure 5D, upper).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: By comparing the positive PI values (greater than zero) between OFF and ON epochs in the three genotypes, the optogenetic activation of T3 neurons was the only perturbation to produce a significant drop in performance.
source: By comparing the positive PI values (greater than zero) between OFF and ON epochs in the three genotypes, the optogenetic activation of T3 neurons was the only perturbation to produce a significant drop in performance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3>CsChrimson flies showed on average an increase frequency of saccades during OFF epochs relative to ON epochs.
source: We next assessed how frequently saccades were triggered under CsChrimson perturbation. T3>CsChrimson flies showed on average an increase frequency of saccades during OFF epochs relative to ON epochs, whereas the frequency of saccades was similar across ON/OFF phases for T4/T5 activated flies and Empty>CsChrimson controls (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The frequency of saccades was similar across ON/OFF phases for T4/T5 activated flies and Empty>CsChrimson controls.
source: We next assessed how frequently saccades were triggered under CsChrimson perturbation. T3>CsChrimson flies showed on average an increase frequency of saccades during OFF epochs relative to ON epochs, whereas the frequency of saccades was similar across ON/OFF phases for T4/T5 activated flies and Empty>CsChrimson controls (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Population depolarization of T3 neurons perturbed the visual pathway supporting bar-evoked saccades.
source: These results indicate that, in agreement with the PI results (Figure 5E and F), population depolarization of T3 neurons perturbed the visual pathway supporting bar-evoked saccades.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When the optogenetic stimulus was switched OFF, recovery from sustained non-selective depolarization strongly revived saccadic bar tracking in flies expressing channelrhodopsin in T3.
source: Yet, when the optogenetic stimulus was switched OFF, recovery from sustained non-selective depolarization strongly revived saccadic bar tracking in flies expressing channelrhodopsin in T3 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T3>CsChrimson flies starting with an OFF epoch showed a slightly higher saccade rate than controls, suggesting that these flies had a higher baseline saccade rate, rather than any CsChrimson activation rebound effect.
source: T3>CsChrimson flies starting with an OFF epoch showed a slightly higher saccade rate than controls, suggesting that these flies had a higher baseline saccade rate, rather than any CsChrimson activation rebound effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: This elevated baseline saccade could reasonably be due to tonic subthreshold depolarization of T3 by the LED display, which could amplify intrinsic synaptic inputs to T3.
source: This elevated baseline saccade could reasonably be due to tonic subthreshold depolarization of T3 by the LED display, which could amplify intrinsic synaptic inputs to T3.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In T3>CsChrimson flies the saccade rate dropped during every ON epoch, and increased during every OFF epoch in a push–pull manner, regardless of the random initial condition.
source: Irrespective of the small elevated baseline saccade rate, in T3>CsChrimson flies the saccade rate dropped during every ON epoch, and increased during every OFF epoch in a push–pull manner, regardless of the random initial condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: No such changes were evident in control or T4/T5>CsChrimson flies.
source: By contrast, no such changes were evident in control or T4/T5>CsChrimson flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Light-gated depolarization of T3 significantly shortened the duration and number of saccades per bout.
source: We next extracted the bouts of bar tracking behavior. Light-gated depolarization of T3 significantly shortened the duration and number of saccades per bout (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: T4/T5>CsChrimson flies showed stronger smooth responses to bar motion (thereby destabilizing large-field optomotor gaze control).
source: T4/T5>CsChrimson flies showed stronger smooth responses to bar motion (thereby destabilizing large-field optomotor gaze control, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Normal T3 function is required for triggering saccades to track moving bars.
source: These results indicate that normal T3 function is required for triggering saccades to track moving bars (Figure 4, Figure 5B–F), but the control of their dynamics is likely modulated by both T3 and T4/T5 neurons as well as by some other unidentified neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The control of saccade dynamics is likely modulated by both T3 and T4/T5 neurons as well as by some other unidentified neurons.
source: These results indicate that normal T3 function is required for triggering saccades to track moving bars (Figure 4, Figure 5B–F), but the control of their dynamics is likely modulated by both T3 and T4/T5 neurons as well as by some other unidentified neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The relatively weak effect on saccade dynamics might be spurious stimulus artifacts, considering the fact that saccade speed, amplitude, and duration are pretty stereotyped in either magnetically tethered and freely flying flies.
source: The relatively weak effect on saccade dynamics might be spurious stimulus artifacts, considering the fact that saccade speed, amplitude, and duration are pretty stereotyped in either magnetically tethered and freely flying flies (Fry et al., 2003; Mongeau and Frye, 2017; Muijres et al., 2015), and that, once triggered, saccades are not influenced by visual feedback (Bender and Dickinson, 2006a).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data supported by citations.

claim: Once triggered, saccades are not influenced by visual feedback.
source: The relatively weak effect on saccade dynamics might be spurious stimulus artifacts, considering the fact that saccade speed, amplitude, and duration are pretty stereotyped in either magnetically tethered and freely flying flies (Fry et al., 2003; Mongeau and Frye, 2017; Muijres et al., 2015), and that, once triggered, saccades are not influenced by visual feedback (Bender and Dickinson, 2006a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Flies execute distinct classes of saccades (i.e., different polarity, amplitude, and duration) for bar tracking, small object aversion, and large-field perturbations.
source: Flies execute distinct classes of saccades (i.e., different polarity, amplitude, and duration) for bar tracking, small object aversion, and large-field perturbations (Mongeau et al., 2019; Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If T3 functions selectively for bar tracking saccades, then perturbing them would have no influence over large-field saccades.
source: To test whether T3 signals are used principally or exclusively to trigger bar tracking saccades, we tested flies with a rotating large-field panorama without a bar object (Figure 6A). Our prediction was that if T3 functions selectively for bar tracking saccades, then perturbing them would have no influence over large-field saccades.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis being tested.

claim: The number of large-field optomotor saccades executed by T3>CsChrimson flies did not change significantly between OFF and ON epochs.
source: In support of this prediction, the number of large-field optomotor saccades executed by T3>CsChrimson flies did not change significantly between OFF and ON epochs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Small increases during ON epochs were shown by Empty>CsChrimson and T4/T5>CsChrimson flies, suggesting to us that the red light was likely triggering startle responses.
source: However, small increases during ON epochs were shown by Empty>CsChrimson and T4/T5>CsChrimson flies, suggesting to us that the red light was likely triggering startle responses (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures, with a speculative interpretation.

claim: T4/T5>CsChrimson flies showed a higher percentage of no stabilization trials compared to Empty>CsChrimson and T3>CsChrimson flies.
source: As expected, T4/T5>CsChrimson flies showed a higher percentage of no stabilization trials compared to Empty>CsChrimson and T3>CsChrimson flies (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: Controls and T3 activated flies showed no effect in the performance between OFF and ON epochs, while T4/T5 activated flies were more inclined to increase the PI during ON than OFF epochs.
source: Considering only positive PI, controls and T3 activated flies showed no effect in the performance between OFF and ON epochs, while T4/T5 activated flies were more inclined to increase the PI during ON than OFF epochs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The perturbation of T4/T5 neurons could alter the normal performance either by driving an abrupt change in the steering direction or by dramatically increasing the smooth optomotor response.
source: This means that the perturbation of T4/T5 neurons could alter the normal performance either by driving an abrupt change in the steering direction or by dramatically increasing the smooth optomotor response (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The effects of T3>CsChrimson are manifest only in the execution of bar tracking saccades.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate, as expected, that T4/T5>CsChrimson perturbs gaze stabilization in response to both a bar and large-field displacements, whereas the effects of T3>CsChrimson are manifest only in the execution of bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: T4/T5>CsChrimson perturbs gaze stabilization in response to both a bar and large-field displacements.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate, as expected, that T4/T5>CsChrimson perturbs gaze stabilization in response to both a bar and large-field displacements, whereas the effects of T3>CsChrimson are manifest only in the execution of bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Flies expressing CsChrimson in T3 and T4/T5 but not exposed to the red light for optogenetic activation showed a higher saccade rate for bar tracking than controls.
source: Interestingly, flies expressing CsChrimson in T3 and T4/T5 but not exposed to the red light for optogenetic activation showed a higher saccade rate for bar tracking than controls, which is the opposite behavior shown by the same driver lines expressing Kir2.1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and figures.

claim: The visual display was sufficient to evoke depolarization of T3 and T4/T5, causing enhanced responses to visual cues and combining to improve saccadic bar tracking.
source: Apparently, the visual display was sufficient to evoke depolarization of T3 and T4/T5, causing enhanced responses to visual cues and combining to improve saccadic bar tracking.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In T4/T5 this effect facilitated gaze stabilization to enable efficient integration of bar error, whereas in T3 the integration itself was enhanced.
source: We reckon that in T4/T5 this effect facilitated gaze stabilization to enable efficient integration of bar error, whereas in T3 the integration itself was enhanced.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Bar tracking saccades are triggered neither by absolute retinal position nor by bar velocity, but rather by a threshold in the spatial integral of bar position over time (integrated retinal position error, Irpe).
source: Prior work has shown that bar tracking saccades are triggered neither by absolute retinal position nor by bar velocity, but rather by a threshold in the spatial integral of bar position over time (Mongeau and Frye, 2017), or integrated retinal position error (Irpe).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For bar tracking saccades, the fixed Irpe is the product of time (inter-saccadic interval [ISI]) and angular distance traveled by the bar with respect to the fly's heading (pre-saccadic error angle).
source: Therefore, for bar tracking saccades, the fixed Irpe is the product of time (inter-saccadic interval [ISI]) and angular distance traveled by the bar with respect to the fly's heading (pre-saccadic error angle).
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: ISI and pre-saccadic error angle terms are inversely proportional, and Irpe is invariant across bar speed.
source: Accordingly, ISI and pre-saccadic error angle terms are inversely proportional, and Irpe is invariant across bar speed (Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When the bar moves fast, the ISI is short and the pre-saccadic error angle is large.
source: When the bar moves fast, the ISI is short and the pre-saccadic error angle is large.
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: When the bar moves slowly, the ISI is extended and the pre-saccadic error angle is reduced.
source: When the bar moves slowly, the ISI is extended and the pre-saccadic error angle is reduced (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: T3's bar-driven calcium responses support a spatiotemporal integrate-and-fire model of bar tracking behavior.
source: We tested whether T3's bar-driven calcium responses support a spatiotemporal integrate-and-fire model of bar tracking behavior.
evidence: This is a statement of the hypothesis being tested.

claim: Calcium signals generated by retinotopic columnar T3 neurons are temporally integrated to reach firing threshold.
source: Our hypothesis is that calcium signals generated by retinotopic columnar T3 neurons are temporally integrated to reach firing threshold.
evidence: This is a statement of the hypothesis being tested.

claim: The number of retinal facets, corresponding neural columns, and T3 neurons that are stimulated by bar motion is proportional to bar speed and inversely related to the visual dwell time and stimulation intensity of T3.
source: The number of retinal facets, corresponding neural columns, and T3 neurons that are stimulated by bar motion is proportional to bar speed and inversely related to the visual dwell time and stimulation intensity of T3.
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: For a downstream integrating neuron, short dwell time corresponds to a low-amplitude signal from any given columnar input, requiring many such signals to charge the integrator to threshold.
source: For a downstream integrating neuron, short dwell time corresponds to a low-amplitude signal from any given columnar input, requiring many such signals to charge the integrator to threshold.
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: If the bar moves slowly, larger amplitude signals mean fewer are needed to reach firing threshold.
source: If the bar moves slowly, larger amplitude signals mean fewer are needed to reach firing threshold.
evidence: This is a statement of the relationship between variables in the model.

claim: This simple scheme would require neural responses that are inversely proportional to bar speed, which is what we observed in T3.
source: This simple scheme would require neural responses that are inversely proportional to bar speed, which is what we observed in T3 (Figure 1I, Figure 7B): low-amplitude calcium responses to fast-moving bars, and large responses to slow-moving bars.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and the model.

claim: Activity of the T3 cell array would be summed by a downstream integrator to the firing threshold for triggering a saccade.
source: Presumably, activity of the T3 cell array would be summed by a downstream integrator to the firing threshold for triggering a saccade (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a statement of the proposed model.

claim: This integrated-and-fired mechanism alone does not explain the reduced ISI with increasing bar speed observed in the behavioral data since T3 inputs would be integrated over a quite constant time window.
source: This integrated-and-fired mechanism alone, however, does not explain the reduced ISI with increasing bar speed observed in the behavioral data since T3 inputs would be integrated over a quite constant time window (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a limitation of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: A simulated fly's angular position based on this physiologically inspired control system with stereotyped saccade amplitudes and a frontal narrow region of space within which no integration takes place can mimic real fly behavior recapitulating a constant Irpe.
source: Despite that, a simulated fly's angular position based on this physiologically inspired control system with stereotyped saccade amplitudes and a frontal narrow region of space within which no integration takes place can mimic real fly behavior recapitulating a constant Irpe (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by modeling and simulation.

claim: This simple model provides a parsimonious explanation for how T3 neurons could provide behaviorally relevant signals to trigger bar tracking saccades.
source: This simple model provides a parsimonious explanation for how T3 neurons could provide behaviorally relevant signals to trigger bar tracking saccades.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental data.

claim: Columnar T3 neurons are small-field (local) detectors of the features contained within stimuli that flies readily track during flight.
source: With this work, we show that (i) columnar T3 neurons are small-field (local) detectors of the features contained within stimuli that flies readily track during flight (Figures 1 and 2), (ii) the integration of these local signals could support the integrated error computations that flies make to track bars (Figure 7), which (iii) can explain why manipulation of T3 function compromises bar tracking saccades (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The integration of T3 local signals could support the integrated error computations that flies make to track bars.
source: With this work, we show that (i) columnar T3 neurons are small-field (local) detectors of the features contained within stimuli that flies readily track during flight (Figures 1 and 2), (ii) the integration of these local signals could support the integrated error computations that flies make to track bars (Figure 7), which (iii) can explain why manipulation of T3 function compromises bar tracking saccades (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data and modeling.

claim: Manipulation of T3 function compromises bar tracking saccades.
source: With this work, we show that (i) columnar T3 neurons are small-field (local) detectors of the features contained within stimuli that flies readily track during flight (Figures 1 and 2), (ii) the integration of these local signals could support the integrated error computations that flies make to track bars (Figure 7), which (iii) can explain why manipulation of T3 function compromises bar tracking saccades (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Flies use smooth optomotor movements to stabilize gaze and to maintain visual course control during locomotion.
source: Like virtually every animal with image forming eyes, including humans, flies use smooth optomotor movements to stabilize gaze and to maintain visual course control during locomotion (Land, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Optomotor stabilization reflexes in flies are elicited by patterns of large-field optic flow that is detected by spatially integrating the signals from two identified classes of directionally selective motion detecting columnar neurons, T4 and T5.
source: It is widely accepted that optomotor stabilization reflexes in flies are elicited by patterns of large-field optic flow that is detected by spatially integrating the signals from two identified classes of directionally selective motion detecting columnar neurons, T4 and T5, that have narrow RFs (small-field) that retinotopically sample the entire visual field (Mauss and Borst, 2020; Yang and Clandinin, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LPTCs have complex directional RFs that act as spatial filters for the patterns of optic flow generated by specific flight maneuvers, and which in turn coordinate smooth optomotor responses.
source: LPTCs have complex directional RFs that act as spatial filters for the patterns of optic flow generated by specific flight maneuvers, and which in turn coordinate smooth optomotor responses (Busch et al., 2018; Krapp and Hengstenberg, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Flies execute saccades to shift gaze, both during walking and in flight to track or avoid salient moving objects.
source: In parallel with smooth continuous optomotor movements, flies, like humans, also execute saccades to shift gaze, both during walking (Geurten et al., 2014) and in flight to track or avoid salient moving objects (Mongeau et al., 2019; Mongeau and Frye, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Models of motion-dependent frontal bar fixation do not account for saccadic object pursuit.
